utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let the witness be brought into court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness is brought in, if I may just address -- if I just may address time limitations issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As I spoke with my learned friend Bakrac today he has at least another half an hour, 35 minutes for cross, and I'm afraid that another hour won't be enough for the rest of us three Defences to finish their cross. So we ask for your leniency on this issue today and to grant at least another half an hour for the Defence cross in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was having regard earlier to the need to break to set up arrangements for the next witness and was hoping that things would fit together neatly. If that's not going to be possible, then it's not going to be possible and we'll just have to proceed as best we can. So we will recognise your need for cross-examination extension, as long as it's plain that what's happening is relevant to the issues that are material to the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pesic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your evidence will now continue. The cross-examination by Mr. Bakrac will continue. Please remember that the solemn declaration to speak the truth continues to apply to your evidence today. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not to use up too much time. I just want to try to convince you - and you can see that from my notes - that I revised my questions and deleted a lot of them, but still a number remain outstanding that I have to ask. Your Honours, you can see the deletions on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pesic, good afternoon. We will continue where we left off last night. If I remember well, I asked you about the forward command post in Djakovica and I would like to know -- or, rather, you said in your statement that in April and May 1999 you were in Djakovica at this forward command post. Is it correct that at that time you did not see General Lazarevic in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in view of the fact that the forward command post existed there was no need for the corps commander to be at the forward command post; that's why it was set up in the first place?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, we will now move on to another subject concerning command and the issuing of orders. We saw yesterday that beginning with the 8th of April, 1999, the military district was resubordinated to the Pristina Corps. Can you tell me after the 8th of April, 1999, from whom did you receive assignments, missions, decisions, orders, to whom were you subordinated?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You mean General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive from General Lazarevic either a verbal or written order that would have been contrary to the law or the basic rules of engagement of the Army of Yugoslavia in peacetime or in wartime?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were shown a Prosecution exhibit - to save time we will not go back to it - it is that document, and for the record I'll tell you the number, P1968. The letterhead says Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Did you ever during the war as the largest unit subordinated to the Pristina Corps ever receive a document headed "Joint Command," an order or any other enactment?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just forgot to ask you very briefly, in paragraph 34 of your statement you spoke of a report that allegedly members of military territorial unit in Istok had formed a camp for Albanian refugees, and you stated that a commission had been established and that together with that commission you went there to inspect. However, we don't know the outcome of that because all you said was that details could be found in a book. In order not to look for that book, just tell us what was the finding of that commission? Was there a camp for Albanian refugees or no?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not a camp, there was no camp, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there any irregularities in the work of military territorial units in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's precisely the military territorial unit in Istok that was commended for their overall activity from the moment of mobilisation until the moment when the commission interviewed the relevant persons from that detachment and their superior command, which was the section in Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Speaking of the sector in Pec, I'll skip a couple of questions and ask you to comment on an exhibit that is in the possession of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we place in e-court 5D36.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you see this document, Mr. Pesic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lettering is very small. Can we zoom in a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I would appreciate that too. This is an order from the command of the military district of Pec signed by Colonel, or rather, Lieutenant-Colonel Dusko Antic. And in paragraph 1 we read the following: "All republican and municipal authorities shall be placed under the command of the Pec VO on the territory of Klina and Decani, among others."

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see this order of my superior because it's not even regular practice for an order to be -- for an order written for subordinates to be forwarded to the superior as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this reaction and was it the result of this reaction that an order arrived nullifying this order? Do you know of this response?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we place in e-court 5D37.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction in line 23, page 4, "I did not see this order of my subordinate," not superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you see this order, another one from Dusko Antic, commander of the military district of Pec, dated the 25th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same answer applies. It's not the practice to forward such orders to the superior. He wrote this order on the basis of a superior order in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you agree that as soon as an irregularity was noticed by the Pristina Corps, there was an immediate response and an order was written to nullify the previous one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that question misstates this document. This appears to be the order from the military district command rather than from the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I asked Mr. Pesic earlier if -- because you see that at that time -- you see the date, 25th of April, 1999, the military district was subordinated to the Pristina Corps. I asked him is it the case that as soon as the Pristina Corps noticed this irregularity an order was issued to nullify the previous one? And I believe the witness answered affirmatively that this order did indeed arrive as a result, both from the Pristina Corps and the military district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question hasn't been answered and the objection is that this appears to be an order from the military district, and indeed is pursuant to another order of the military district command. And is not an order from the Pristina Corps. Now, what's your response to that? That means that the question is not formulated in an appropriate way. It's your answer I'm looking for, Mr. Bakrac. What is your answer to the point that is being made that this is not an order of the Pristina Corps nor is it implementing an order of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I understood that. The order -- I don't quite understand you. I asked the witness whether this order whereby the commander of the military district of Pec nullifies his previous order was a result of the reaction of the Pristina Corps and the command of the military district to an irregularity that had been observed in the previous order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether there's something wrong with interpretation or translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, there isn't. First of all, I don't understand what the irregularity is and it would be helpful to know that; and secondly, you've now compiled what appears to be a multiple question, relating to both the Pristina Corps and the military district of Pec. So I have to say that I'm very confused about this and therefore I will sustain the objection. You ought to formulate questions which are clear and helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am struggling with the time limitations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, may I make a remark about that. Subject to this point, which may actually be additional information, you've only asked one question so far that's added to my knowledge of this case, and that question was whether this witness had ever received any document headed "Joint Command." Nothing else you've asked, with great respect, has added to our knowledge of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, I've shown you already these two orders. There's no need to go back to them. Is it true that on the 30th of March, 1999, the commander of the military sector of Pec issued an order that went beyond his legal powers, whereby municipal authorities were placed under the command of the military sector of Pec?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was this irregularity noticed and where, by whom?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the corps and the command of the military sector, and he did indeed react, the commander did react in this order 139-387/1 of the 25th of April, and then this commander in question issued another order nullifying that previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on. Would you agree with me that the commander of the military district, that is you as the commander of the military district, issued orders to your units but not regarding use of troops in combat? I'm talking about the moment when the military sector was resubordinated to the corps.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly there were some orders that governed matters of life and work of units, and there are such orders. But it was all in view of the overall situation, not daily contacts with the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it true that those orders of yours were a result of efforts and insistence by the Pristina Corps command that the laws and Geneva Conventions be abided by in the operation of the corps and its subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. It's possible that this order also came from the corps via the 125th Brigade, who had Pec in their zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the registrar to place 5D32 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, do you recognise this order signed by commander Colonel Zlatomir Pesic? Is it your order? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's an order of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Again, to save time, I'll summarise what's written here. It's in evidence. Is it true that the point of this order is care and protection for the civilian population in case of clashes with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: True. But it's possible that the military sector also got this order through the command of the 125th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I noticed in the transcript that there is one reference missing in my question. I said in case of clashes with the KLA and NATO bombing, NATO bombing was missed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, let's move on. Do you remember the order of the Pristina Corps issued in late April regulating the issue of stabilising lines of defence and the accent was put on the defence of the lines, relationship with the civilian population, and the undertaking of measures against perpetrators of criminal offences amongst the ranks of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the registrar to put 5D35 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you look at the first and last pages. My question is: Does this order comprise the topics I've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And please let us see the last page where we have the signature and the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And it reads "Colonel Zlatomir Pesic."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: For Colonel Zlatomir Pesic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the answer was yes, that's the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5D38 put on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, can you see this order dated the 30th of March, 1999, signed by commander Colonel Zlatomir Pesic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an order of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does the first item read: "Fully abide by the regulations on the application of the international laws of war within the VJ, the issue of the administration of the federal secretariat for defence of 1998"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This handbook had been distributed to the members of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that item 3 reads: "Against those violating the provisions of the international laws of war, their superiors are duty-bound to initiate proceedings in order to apply sanctions prescribed by the law"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let us try and rush through to try and conclude shortly. The next question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, is there an English version available? I'm only seeing two B/C/S on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English translation has been inserted in the system. I don't think whether this is a technical hitch, but we do have the translation. We put it in the system and we notified the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy of the English version available that you can give to Mr. Hannis just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we received it yesterday, or this morning, and during the break I'll try to provide a copy for Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, is it correct that with the military district there was a military prosecutor as well as a military judge as part of the military district? Excuse me, the military court. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it had its own prosecutor and judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was there a separate military court and prosecutor of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a separate one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, the military district of Pristina had their own prosecutor and judge?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in wartime after mobilisation is carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the military prosecutor of the military district of Pristina and its military district were subordinated to the supreme military court in Belgrade and not to the military prosecutor and the military court of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain whether they were subordinated to Belgrade, but in any case they were subordinated to Nis. I'm not familiar with the judicial hierarchy. As for the 3rd Army command where there was a court, I know of that but nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But the essence, the gist, of my question is whether the military prosecutor and court of the military district were not subordinated to the military court of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, I'm about to complete my cross-examination but I would like to know this first. Did you know that the military prosecutor instituted proceedings in case of violations of law -- of the law against certain members of units of the military district and do you know whether this was seen through by the military courts of the district?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both the prosecutor and the court were in operation as of day one. They processed a number of cases during the bombings and they've also completed a number of cases after the bombings ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you agree with me that, be it yourself or the Pristina Corps, whenever you found out there was a violation of some -- of members of the units belonging to the military district that you instituted proceedings against those people and that they were tried?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I was trying to state, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he can answer whether he himself did it but I don't know if he can answer for the Pristina Corps. The question was: "Can you agree with me that, be it yourself or the Pristina Corps, whenever you found out that there was a violation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Pristina Corps required that measures be taken against members of the units of the military district in terms of instituting proceedings against such people for the crimes perpetrated?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the military district was subordinated to the Pristina Corps there was a close cooperation of the security organs, and as part of that cooperation they did that as well. There were such cases. But as to whether these cases were forwarded to either the military prosecutor of the district or of the Pristina Corps, I don't know precisely. But there were such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the military prosecutor and court of the military district were competent to try members of the military district who had committed crimes and offences instead of the court of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My last question will be this, and then I will ask the Bench to try and identify four or five documents so as to be able to move more quickly. Perhaps we can just ask the witness to identify the documents and then I would like to conclude and I believe this would save us some time. Mr. Pesic, I have one last question on this topic. Is it correct - and I would like to know that because of another witness who is to come here and testify - that on the 30th of May, 1999, there was an incident between the military prosecutor and his deputy, who were members of the military district?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you any details and a lot of time has elapsed. I spoke to both of them. It was of a rather personal nature, I'd say. The -- one or the other was ignorant of something that was discussed. I don't know whether it was linked to a particular case or not. I believe it concerned a certain person who had been appointed, but I don't know any more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say a particular person, was this -- was this Djorovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What do you mean by a peculiar person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's an odd translation, I think. It concerned a certain or a particular person. I don't think the witness was referring to an unusual person, was he?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to go again. Lakic Djorovic was the name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, perhaps the counsel should be asked to specify whether he means specific or peculiar person. It is unclear from B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you said an odd, a strange person, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he didn't say odd or strange as far as I see. It's translated as particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's nothing wrong with the question. The witness should be able to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I believe there was a misinterpretation. We speak the same language and we understand each other. I know what the witness had in mind. He didn't have in mind a particular but a peculiar, an odd person but the witness can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would prefer the translation from the official translator to that effect rather than Mr. Bakrac's translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I think if you had just allowed the witness to answer the last question that was asked the position would have been clarified. Now, the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you really can tell us anything useful about this at all. What the witness has said is that this was some personal dispute between the two of them. Is that relevant to the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, I believe it is. It concerns a witness who is to appear here on behalf of the OTP and we are going to test his credibility. This witness cooperated with that person, and I'm trying to gain some useful information from this witness, if he's got anything to say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pesic, we better go back to square one. Tell us what you know about this dispute between the prosecutor and his deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know very little, Mr. Bonomy. I tried to familiarise myself with the case, and I spoke to both of them. And that's why I said that these are difficult people who didn't know each other. One of them had been there for some time, whereas Mr. Lakic was sent from Nis. He was appointed to that position. They didn't know each other, and they couldn't get on well. Somebody wanted to smoke at his table. Somebody was a rowdy person. Somebody had an inclination to drink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, we need to get to the point, please. If you know more about it, please put a direct question that's going to make some progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Well, I don't seem to have received much from this --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say "prone to alcohol," what did you have in mind, Djorovic Lakic, did he have a reputation of someone who drinks?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. And a judge from Nis came by the name of Radosavljevic and he tried to deal with the case, and the person was replaced and the business went on as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pesic. I have one last question and then I wanted to go through the exercise of identifying documents, so as to be able to tender them. Mr. Pesic, is it correct - and when you spoke about uniforms - that the uniforms of the Pristina Corps units were, for the most part, green camouflage M-89 or M-93, and there were a few of the olive-green-grey type, the SMB type, which were M-77. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to put Exhibit 5D34 on the screen, pages 1 and 2, where the signature is so as to see whether the witness recognises it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document, Mr. Pesic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the first page, since I believe you were able to see the signature.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document? Is this a document of yours? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It's your document?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the registrar to put 5D39 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document? It's signed deputy commander Colonel Zivojin Djaklic? It's an order prohibiting theft, looting, robbing.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask Exhibit 5D41 to be placed on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 1 of this document, then we'll move on to the signature and the second page.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we zoom in a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, could we please zoom in a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you see better now?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we move on -- scroll down, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: These are reports concerning the work of the military court. We don't have time to go into detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I inquire, is there an English version available of this one? I don't seem to have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Yes, Your Honour. There is an English version. Everything has been translated and placed on e-court. It must be a technical problem. I'll note it down and try to resolve it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see it now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, please look at the signature and the stamp. Is it your document?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now have 5D42 placed in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, can you see the first page of this document dated 18th May 1991 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Again, it's about the measures to be taken --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an error in the transcript on -- in line 25. We see 1991 instead of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we move on to page 2, Mr. Pesic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you see the signature and the stamp? Is it your document?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was signed by my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Which deputy?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Djaklic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And the last document I want to show you in conclusion is 5D43.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it please be shown on e-court. Can you zoom in a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you see the first page? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In para 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can scroll down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: -- do we see precisely a reference to the conflict between the prosecutor, the military prosecutor, Lieutenant-Colonel Lakic Djorovic, and the deputy of the military prosecutor, para 4. Is it written here that the incident was caused by the said prosecutor Lakic Djorovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see then page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions. And I don't know whether it is technically necessary for me to repeat the numbers of these exhibits before I tender them because the witness authenticated them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are exhibits which are documents of the witness which appear to be relevant -- or of his department which appear to be relevant to issues in the case and therefore will be exhibited in their entirety. I have one question arising out of the last document and that is: What was the result of the investigation into the fight between the prosecutor and his deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Lakic was replaced by another man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Pesic. My name is Branko Lukic. I appear before this Tribunal on behalf of General Lukic. I would be grateful if you could help me clarify certain points.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we first see P1326 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for this to be placed on the screen, it's a set of photographs depicting uniforms. And I'll have a couple of questions. By way of introduction, I would say that you said yesterday that the army had uniforms marked as M-77, M-80, M-90, M-91, and we heard today that there were also uniforms M-89 and M-93. On this photograph which is a Prosecution exhibit, do you recognise military uniforms, Mr. Pesic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photographs are blurry, but on picture 7 -- sorry, 9, I recognise military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we enlarge this picture starting with 1, please, moving on to 2 and so on. And we need to see the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photographs are not very clear, and picture number 9 is the only one that seems to me to depict members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So these uniforms that you enumerated M-77, M-80, M-90, M-91, M-89, M-93 are not to be seen among the uniforms depicted on this set of photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that form of the question. He's indicated the pictures are blurry, so that doesn't necessarily mean that the uniforms aren't depicted there. He's just saying the pictures are blurry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a question the witness could answer. He could have given the answer that you've just given, Mr. Hannis. There was nothing wrong with that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, we received this set of photographs from the Prosecution and it was said they would be used during your examination. Were they shown to you during proofing?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about photographs 1 and 2? Can you make out whether the uniforms shown there are consistent with military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently they remind me of military photographs. I can't see clearly, that's about picture 1. And on picture 2 what we see could be the grey-olive-green or it could be bluish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we quickly show pictures 3, 4, and 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Number 3?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll see 5 very soon. Number 5?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly it could be one of them, 89 or 93, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about number 6?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see number 7, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Number 8?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Number 9? You said already this was a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than any of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about 10?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. This is 10.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never had occasion to see this type of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's the KLA uniform.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But in any case on this set of photographs, not all uniforms you designated as uniforms worn by the Army of Yugoslavia are shown?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are in a bit of a hurry, as you know. We've heard that the Pristina Military District consisted of five military sectors. How many military territorial detachments were there? Because we have two diverging numbers.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 24 detachments and one artillery battalion of the anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the Pristina Military District? How many members did it have in end March 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: End March 1999. Does the figure 4.000 sound right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many were there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't quite understand the question because the detachments were mobilised one after the other in succession, and I have documentation showing when I mobilised the first two and then the next ones, up to six or eight before the beginning of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the maximum strength in the course of 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the entire establishment, over 12.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now something about Lieutenant-General Bojovic. What was his unit called? Was it the administration for defence, the one that he commanded?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, before he was appointed commander of the Pristina Corps, General Bojovic was commander of the provincial staff of the Territorial Defence. That's what I know. At that time I was outside of the province of Kosovo. I was in the 3rd Army in Vranje or Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was Petar Ilic the head of?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He headed one of the bodies of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this body called defence administration?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was defence administration. The provincial administration of the Ministry of Defence. I don't think it's difficult to find a document verifying the exact name of the institution; it existed for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning your agencies, that is the military district, the military territorial sectors, or detachments, were they ever in any way subordinated to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know sometimes questions sound peculiar, but in paragraph 68 of the indictment we read that your body, among others, was subordinated to the MUP. Therefore, I would ask you to bear with me even when I'm asking questions that sound peculiar to you. What happened military territorial detachments, did they exist in the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly. I've already said. I told you, even the smallest municipality had one of the detachments, that is, a reduced detachment. At least a company of B classification, B category.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about some municipalities, if you can recall any details pertaining that them. In Djakovica, what was your formation there and who commanded it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Djakovica there was a detachment, one detachment, which had not been brought up to strength. It comprised only two companies. The commander was an active-duty officer, lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you cannot recall that's fine. How about Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a detachment in Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Pristina, how many military territorial detachments?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One territorial detachment, the 115th, then the artillery battalion of the anti-aircraft defence, and one reconnaissance sabotage department, then -- detachment, then a communications company and an engineering company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Kosovo Polje, what formation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to put this in proper context in terms of time. There was the 115th and the reconnaissance sabotage one at a certain point, as well as the anti-aircraft artillery battalion. But at a certain point they were issued other tasks and they moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How about Klina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One detachment comprising two companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Istok?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No detachments, or rather, the detachment in Urosevac pulled out the people from Kacanik and used them and the Urosevac people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Vitina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a Vitina detachment and they all have -- each of the detachments had their own designator.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, designation in terms of establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you recall what was the manning strength, the number of conscripts in the registry of the Pristina Military District, total number?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you asked me that one. The entire military district, as I said, if brought up to full strength, but it varied nevertheless because we had to relieve some and then mobilise some others, but in any case the figure was around or slightly over 12.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is as concerns the military territorial detachments, but I may have been imprecise. I wanted to know the total number of conscripts for all units.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All conscripts for Kosovo, well, I don't know. But it is in the documentation. We have the able-bodied men, the conscripts, but I can't tell you any figures. And my deputy was in charge of that in particular. It was the assistant for the military service. He had his own lists, and I cannot give you an estimate. I was a new person in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I tried to see if you can recollect. Thank you in any case. Yesterday we talked about different age of conscripts. What about reservists? Were they sent to both -- to the police and the army irrespective of their age? Was there a distinction made or not in terms of age as to who would go where?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never sent them to the police. We only sent them to serve their military term.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the reservists who were sent to the police and to the army, were they of the same age?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there was a possibility of choice. In peacetime the military district commands and the MUP would hand-pick people if they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on their specialty and not on their age, I presume?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, their specialty was the deciding factor. As for their age, well, they wanted to have younger men but it depended on their agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On both parties, I presume?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we tried to deal with everything that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Bakrac asked you about a document, and I believe something remains unclear for the Court as well. I will try to clarify this further. It is 5D36. It concerns the municipality of Pec, and we've established that there was something wrong with the document. When going through it, we see that on the 30th of March, 1999, the military sector of Pec command in item 1 orders that all republican and municipal authorities be put under the command of the military sector Pec in the territories of municipalities of Pec, Istok, Klina, and Decani. Is this the irregularity we referred to? Because one of the republican organs is the MUP as well.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it because of this attempt to resubordinate units of the MUP? What caused discontent within the MUP and there was resistance on their part for the units to be resubordinated in this way. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the commander of the Pec military sector had a good intention in mind here, since he was partly familiar with the Law on All People's Defence. He thought he was the most senior commander in the area and that he could regulate life and work in wartime, life and work of units, forgetting that there was within the area of responsibility of the 125th Brigade. In Pec, according to the peacetime plans, the unit there was the rank of battalion or artillery battalion. It is possible, provided that unit was elsewhere on orders, on a certain task - although I cannot claim that, it could have been ordered by the command of the 125th - then it is possible that the commander of the military sector was right to draft this, because the Law on All People's Defence states that the command of battalion can order or regulate by orders all matters pertaining to life and work of the unit. In keeping with that, the commander of detachment in Istok, who was reserve captain Toplica, issued his order regulating the life and work within the municipality of Istok because the highest-ranking unit was a battalion, and you can find this in the Law on All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the same situation was in the municipality of Istok, something similar was put in place?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we saw subsequently, after almost a month, that order was nullified. We saw that on the 25th of April it was ordered that this particular order be declared null and void by the same Mr. Antic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in the meantime another unit, the rank of brigade, arrived in that territory. I remember Colonel Cirkovic who took over command of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that was after the 18th of April when the order on resubordination was issued?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say, but it was at that time when we were trying to deal with this, and by that time the command of the brigade had regulated the life and work within that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To go back to the uniforms, there's something I missed as for the military territorial detachments. What type of insignia did such units have on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no particular insignia. We wore the uniforms that were there at the time, M-77, -89, -93.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These were all military uniforms. What did you wear on your arms?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about any hats or so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wore berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How were your units billeted? Were they within barracks or did they spend the night at home, and did the same go for all of the locations or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Pesic. The relevance of this to your case, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I would like to hear the answer from this witness, then it would be easy to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought your concern was about the police. Are you telling me that this is relevant to the police position?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Police, but if you look to the indictment this segment is of our concern as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, help me, in what way you see this as a question that's relevant to your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When explaining Mr. Lukic's function on Kosovo and Metohija and his right to command various units under Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is -- you're saying that military units could be commanded by him?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Partially, according to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the paragraph you referred to earlier? 68, wasn't it? I understood you to have already had an answer from the witness that the MUP were never subordinated to the military territorial districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or, vice versa, that they were not subordinated to MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, sorry, the opposite, yes, that the military was never subordinated to the MUP. And is that not the end of the matter? And therefore do you have an interest in the question you've now asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I really do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I trust you to have a relevant basis. Continue. I have to say I find it difficult to see that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to show it afterwards, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pesic, can you tell us whether your people were billeted in barracks or whether they went home overnight.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not billeted in any barracks, not a single unit in Kosovo, because the barracks had been abandoned before the bombings. At first, such units provided security in the barracks because, as I said, they were supposed to secure buildings and important facilities of state importance. But once the barracks had been abandoned, they were given or assigned different locations. When I toured them, I would find them in the areas I knew they were in, based on the reports of commanders. And I usually went to the detachments myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, they were deployed outside of settlements?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside or on the outskirts in order to try and protect themselves from air-raids.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... transcript 31, 8, it says: "But once the barracks had been abandoned." Actually, the witness said when the barracks started being bombed. It can be clarified with the witness. 31, 8, page 31, 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. If you look at 31, 4 and 5, you'll see the barracks had been abandoned before the bombings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but 31, number 8 -- well, I was just -- I just made the comment according to what the witness had said. I understand it comes from the meaning of the whole passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pesic, did you say that the barracks had been bombed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you should be conscious of the need to pause after the answer before you ask your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to be conscious of so many things, so that's why I'm maybe not handling everything properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pesic, when describing the tasks of your units, which, inter alia, included control of territory, can you tell us what territory they controlled and how was it decided, based on what? What territory would be controlled by your units?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on decisions of commanders of the military sectors. The presence of a given unit within a certain municipality comprising several villages would be done in such a way that the commander of the military sector would issue an order to the commander of the detachment. He would assign a specific area, mentioning which villages and property should be secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say they manned check-points as well. Were your units indeed at check-points?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only the military police company was engaged in that. They were commanded by myself and they were in the town of Pristina itself. They cooperated with other organs of the MUP and the military police of the 15th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for traffic regulation, you mentioned that as one of the tasks. I don't know whether it came about.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not directly. They were at check-points in cooperation with the organs of the MUP and the command of the 15th Brigade within which AOR Pristina was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying abbreviate this to the extent possible. Yesterday my colleague Mr. O'Sullivan asked you about a meeting attended by Mr. Milutinovic, and we had occasion to see that you remembered the meeting but not all the details, so I'll try to refresh your memory a little. Would you agree with me that it was a brief visit and a brief address by the president of Serbia of about 45 minutes to a certain number of members of both sectors of the Army of Yugoslavia after the rest of the schedule had been dealt with and before the lunch, and that everything took place in the building of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was very brief. I don't think there was a single question from the audience.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe it doesn't matter, but let us try. You said you were in the fourth row and that there were about 20 people; however, we have information that there were 79 people. To avoid confusion later, can you remember the number?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When General Pavkovic and I came, there was a smaller number of people present and I believe most of them were members of the MUP, officers of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our information is 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, was it the visit or the address that lasted 45 minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that was about that long, not long. When I sat down I was trying to say there were not many people around, and later on I didn't turn around to see how many more people came in later. Of course when the president came we rose, and it was my impression that there were not many people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me try again. Was it the visit that lasted 45 minutes or was it the address by Mr. Milutinovic that lasted 45 minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I can't give you a precise answer. I believe counsel is right when he says it was short. It was just a short briefing, and there were no -- there was no discussion, no question and answer session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No answer there then, Mr. Lukic. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just another thing, Mr. Pesic. Prosecution Exhibit P1737, we don't need to see it on the screen. It's the Law on Internal Affairs. Since I don't know whether what you said was indeed recorded, I'll try to refresh your memory. Article 28 speaks about the reserve force of the police. Article 28 says: "The minister may summon members of the reserve force to perform certain peacetime tasks from the purview of the ministry, especially to be engaged in activity related to risks to the safety of the republic, restoring public law and order, and in cases of natural disasters. Persons from the reserve force shall be engaged by the minister in tasks from para 1 of this article for as long as safety reasons justify this." Let me ask you first, in 1998 and 1999, were there any safety-related reasons or security-related reasons that would justify the use of the reserve force of the police?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the use of the reserve force of the police -- I'm sorry. I'm getting confused with military terms versus police terms. The use of reserve units, reserve personnel, of the police was justified and existed in Kosovo in 1998/1999?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as 1998 is concerned, I don't know much. I was engaged in other work; and concerning 1999, I know that part of the personnel was indeed mobilised to meet the requirements of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pesic, for answering my questions. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, it's time for me to repay my debt incurred when I -- when I dealt with another witness too long. Now I'm not going to ask any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have questions, but I don't know whether it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How long are you likely to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I just begin? Certainly more than 15 minutes but not longer than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in that case we will break now and we will resume at five past 4.00. Mr. Pesic, we have to break now. Please go with the usher while we have our break and we will see you in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel Pesic. My name is Tomislav Visnjic, attorney-at-law, representing General Ojdanic. I will have a few brief questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd kindly ask for 5D35 to be shown to the witness, page 2, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this question of mine will concern some of your previous answers and the orders issued by Colonel Antic on behalf of the military sector of Pec. Is it correct that by your order you prohibited any issuing of orders by commanders of the units of the military district pertaining to the functioning of the organs of authorities or the so-called Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear of these Crisis Staffs for the first time. As for the first part of your question, it is unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It is paragraph 4, Colonel, of your are document dated the 20th of April, 1999, called measures to stabilise defence, page 2, paragraph 4. It regulates the authorities of the commanders of military units and military -- of the military sector.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Concerning your answer when -- answers when questioned by Mr. Lukic and Bakrac, can we agree that what the commanders of the military district units tried to regulate pertained to the life and work of the particular unit and not on the life and work of entire municipalities or territories?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are no longer within their -- the area of their competence because they had been resubordinated to the military command, and as of that moment the military commander in charge was responsible for all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us have a look at another exhibit, it is 3D429, a regular combat report. Can we go together through this combat report dated the 11th of April, 1999, so as to try and explain to the Bench what took place in one single day in Kosovo. First of all, these regular combat reports, were they being put together as summary reports of the reports you had received from your subordinated units? And at that moment they may have already been resubordinated to the units of the corps but nevertheless sent their reports to you as well.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Based on the reports received, we would compile our own reports sent to the command of the corps. If we learned something after we've drafted a particular report, then such information is included in the next one. Unless there were some extreme or extraordinary situations or circumstances which may be addressed separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at item 1, for the most part it explains or describes the bombing of NATO aircraft -- or performed by NATO aircraft. I wanted us to look at line 6 in Serbian, and it says the targets were the towns of Djakovica, Pec, and Prizren, extensive damage was close to private houses. Djakovica, Pec, and Prizren have a majority Albanian population. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And this part of the report was compiled best on the reports you had received from your territorial units, from these towns?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you to look at paragraph 3 -- or paragraph 3 of item 1. It says: "Several bombs fell on the Goles repeater and on the Merdare pass. These attacks by NATO aircraft and cruise missiles may have caused casualties but this was difficult to establish due to continuous activities of the enemy during the day." Colonel, you often encountered such situations in which certain VJ units and authorities had difficulty in exercising their powers due to NATO air-strikes in the field?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it -- is it because of that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please pause between question and answer. Could Mr. Visnjic please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I correct, Colonel, if I say that due to the danger of being bombed it was impossible to carry out on-site investigations and to establish what the real situation was in the field very often?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have much knowledge from the field, apart from the reports I received. For one to be able to have a full picture, one had to move about, and I agree with you when you say that it was difficult to gain information and to forward that information to your superior as regards the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, please take a look at the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's still first page on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next paragraph where a border incident occurred in the area of Kosare when some 1.000 terrorists with some artillery support attempted an attack from Albania.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we on the wrong page?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are, Your Honour. It is page 1, the fourth paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have page 1 in the English, please, also. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, does this description describe a large offensive initiated by the KLA from Albania in early April, trying to break out to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is based on information of the territorial sector of Pec together with the command of the 125th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you have no reason to dispute or question what is stated here?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. And I forwarded this as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the bottom of page 1, it is said that during the day a Red Cross warehouse was handed over as well as a service Opel, Sicani, and they were handed over to the command of the 202nd Logistics Base. Colonel, was this standard procedure to hand over property?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Cross facility was secured by the engineering company which had been subordinated to me, and as much the facility was on the list of the provincial civilian protection staff. A part of the goods there was distributed to various bodies, including the police and the army. As for the Opel service station called Sicani --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, it is in your statement. I'm not trying to repeat what you've already said. I'm just asking you whether this was the standard procedure for you to hand this over to the 202 logistics base.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, it was based on orders of the commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next page, page 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go to the next page, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Pesic, would you please read for me the first sentence of the paragraph number 1 in the report. Read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Aggressor NATO aircraft, during the night between the 10th and 11th of April, 1999" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it common in a report of this nature to use an expression like "aggressor NATO aircraft" in an official military report?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it a question for witness or for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's the witness I'm asking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is normal for a daily report like this one to be drafted by the team on duty at the operations centre. That team is in charge of collecting data from the field. And it was up to the two people who were there who drafted this report to use this term. This is how they decided to term the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The report in the end of the day, though, is your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, but I wasn't the one who would draft it. It would be drafted by the duty officer, and either I or my assistant would read it through and then forward it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Rather than go to another page, Mr. Visnjic, who actually signed this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was signed by Colonel Pesic on page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So my question, I repeat, Colonel Pesic: Is that normal language for a report of this nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, at that moment I can assure you that was the term used by the duty officer who wrote the report. Of course I did not dictate it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have already told me that. Please answer the question I'm asking you, and if you can't answer it just tell me. Is it normal language for a report of this nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our peacetime practice we have a term that we used to begin with, such as the enemy when speaking of the enemy. In this case, the officer used this term and I didn't pay much attention. It didn't strike me -- although I might even agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's really not my question and it's a pity that you're determined not to answer the question I've put to you, but we need to make progress. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you something about this paragraph 1, Mr. Pesic. Is it customary - and I believe there is a manual on writing reports or a similar document of the Army of Yugoslavia - that para 1 always describes the activity of the enemy. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In reports, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Would I also be right if I said that in almost all reports - I mean combat reports - paragraph 1 described air-strikes by the NATO air force and activities of the KLA forces?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was customary. That was the focus of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may have misunderstood the question, Mr. Visnjic. It's the use of the word "aggressor" that concerned me, not whether there was a reference to NATO. And I just wondered if that's a normal way of describing the attacking force in this type of military report. It's a tendentious comment, and I wonder if that was normal. It's like other expressions we keep seeing in these reports and it's used constantly by counsel here for reasons I find difficult to understand, "the so-called KLA." It seems to be a Balkan tendency to be determined to put in some sort of word that is -- shows a certain bias unnecessarily in the context certainly in which we are dealing with the matter here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know if it would surprise you, but if we go into detail of these documents you'll find that NATO air force is usually referred to as aggressors, and we'll find a lot of documents referring to the aggression of NATO member states against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague Mr. Fila adds that there is even a resolution of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but it's a pity you haven't taken the solemn declaration to speak the truth, Mr. Visnjic, but you've given me the answer I expected I would have got straight away from the witness. But as it turned out, it was a laborious and non-productive exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to page 2, then, Colonel. My colleague Mr. Bakrac showed you a couple of orders which prohibit theft, looting, robbery, and other criminal offences related to property. In paragraph 2, it is said that only on that day 23 persons were detained, taken into custody for misappropriating property. Is this one of the reports that you received almost daily, showing that security agencies were performing their job and taking into custody offenders?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. This is a military police company that only in Pristina in only one day, as on the previous day when the last report was written, and this could be a report covering two days, was doing its job and informing the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you -- can you recollect whether on any occasion during the first half of 1999, when you were writing reports of this nature - or perhaps these are confined to the period after the 23rd of March - but can you recall whether in any you were able to report that any persons had been detained by the military police in connection with allegations of the commission of what might be described as war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, you mean after the beginning of the aggression or until that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, from the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the 23rd of March. I can't remember specific examples, but I can claim - speaking about detachments - that I did not encounter such cases at all. And we had no trials involving such cases before our courts. We had no one in our units charged with war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But you had criminal reports for theft, murder, and similar criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thefts, yes. I don't know about murders. I don't know of any member of a detachment tried for murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question related to paragraph 3. Was a reference to a request to investigate four members of the OSCE verification mission suspected of the crime of espionage.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a case where a security agency of the military district was involved in cooperation with the chief of security of the corps, and that's why it's covered in the report. I think it is a well-known case, though, the trial, but it was a high-profile case, although I don't want to go into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask 3D431 shown to the witness. 3D431.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
