utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, or rather, Colonel, I'd like to ask you this: Yesterday in your testimony you said that the Albanian -- in fact, that you tried to keep one group of Albanians and persuade them to return. As you noticed Albanian civilians leaving, did you also see them returning to their residences once the danger was gone, danger from air-strikes or combat activity?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please then look at this document, 3D431, last paragraph on the first page. The last paragraph on page 1, does it refer to the part of report you received from your territorial units?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to apologise. This is what occurred often. I was there that day. I was present and saw many things, many of those people. Touring the Podujevo detachment, which was securing the water facility in Pristina, I had contact with those people who spent some time in an area a few kilometres away from where the military territorial detachment of Podujevo was, and on that occasion we talked to them. And these people were returning in groups to their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask you again about paragraph 1 of this document in which it is mentioned that NATO aviation attacked a refugee camp in Djakovica, and it is mentioned here that the camp was destroyed completely and that there were casualties among the refugees. There were wounded and killed.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was based on the military sector report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The one from Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no, no, from Prizren, the Prizren military sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 4 of the same page, it is stated that in the Suva Reka municipal territory a shell was fired from a recoilless gun. This is what BST should stand for, if I'm not mistaken, and it is of 82-millimetre calibre?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Whereupon one MUP member was killed and another two seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was also based on the report of the commander of the military sector of Prizren, and apart of the unit was within the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this, since it doesn't seem to be clear from the report, but I believe it is presumed that the KLA used that recoilless gun.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 2 of this document in paragraph 5, it is stated that there was a combat action taken against the KLA and, inter alia, a war diary was found, a war diary of a KLA battalion commander. My question is this: Do you know where that document could be found nowadays?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the military district command was subordinated to the Pristina Corps, the chief of security was supposed to report to the chief of security of the Pristina Corps. And anything that was seized or found should have been turned over to the security chief of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we might be able to find it in the archives of the Pristina Corps or in the security administration?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The security organ of the Pristina Corps, they should have record of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And item 6 of the same page, there is a mention of the difficulties encountered in communicating with your units and that that is why you used couriers for the most part. This is what you've already described in your statement and in your testimony here before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show 3D432 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, it is an order of yours dated the 29th of April, 1999, concerning a ban on the existence of paramilitary formations. The text speaks for itself; therefore, could you just confirm to us whether you issued this order.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, I'll have a few questions about a previous period that you also touch upon in your statement. As I understood from your statement, from 1997 [as interpreted] on you were commander of the artillery battalion within the 549th Brigade. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your commander at the time was Dragoljub Ojdanic. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a colonel then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At that time, how often did you used to see Colonel Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least once a month for a briefing or to submit reports. On some occasions, several times a month, but once at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction for the transcript. It is 1987 rather than 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I had just noted: Quick rise to the top, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your brigade at the time, were there any Albanians serving their military terms or were there any Albanian officers?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, these Albanian officers or soldiers, were they discriminated against in any way for being Albanian?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in no way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: From your knowledge and from the extent you knew Colonel Ojdanic at the time and his style of command, do you think he would have tolerated any sort of discrimination based on ethnic grounds against ethnic Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's an inappropriate question. What sort of answer do you expect anybody to give to that sort of question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you've had a clear answer that there was no discrimination. You then have posed an entirely hypothetical question that we do not think will add anything useful for our purposes, and therefore we will sustain this objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree and I accept that completely. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I have some questions for you on re-direct examination. Yesterday Mr. Bakrac was asking you some questions, and one of the questions was about conscripts who were not mobilised and whether they had been issued uniforms before. Let me find the precise question, the precise wording of that question. It was at page 7247, line 16. Yes,

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC ASKED YOU
utterances.text: "Is it also correct that those who had not been mobilised were those conscripts who had had their uniforms and equipment from an earlier period?" Now, maybe it's my misunderstanding, but I took the term "conscript" to mean someone who had never done military service before and was being called up to do their military service. Am I mistaken about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Explain that to me then. What does "conscript" refer to?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already dealt with that topic. The military obligation lasts from the moment one reaches 18 until 55. It begins with the duty to do military service and then continues into the obligation to be available to the reserve force. I have been asked that by Defence counsel, and I believe that I answered yes. There were certain conscripts who had a wartime assignment but were never mobilised and still kept their uniforms with them because they had never been invited to return the uniform to supplies. They were replaced by younger men in an effort to rejuvenate units, and I believe that there was a question to that effect which I answered. So it was possible to find a uniform in the possession of a person who is a military conscript without a current assignment to a particular unit. The unit could and was supposed to invite him one day to come and return the uniform to supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: Would someone receive a military uniform without having first done their obligation to serve in the military?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Then it's my misunderstanding about the use of the term, of "conscript" versus "reservist." All right. Someone would not have a uniform at home unless they had already done their obligatory military service. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in connection with that question, Mr. Bakrac then asked you whether these conscripts were those who had been issued with uniforms before as reservists before the war. They had it at home, and on page 7248, line 7, he said: "Did you have occasion to see such not mobilised members wearing uniforms?" Your answer was: "It was not unusual to see people, men, wearing parts of uniforms and not complete uniforms." Judge Bonomy asked you a question on the next page about these persons, and Mr. Visnjic helped inform us at page 7249 that you had indicated that those persons you saw with partial uniforms were mostly or mainly unarmed. Did you see any of these individuals wearing partial uniforms carrying military weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not, because such a person would have been immediately noticed by all the competent authorities, the military police and the civilian police if they had both inappropriate clothing and a weapon. In that case, measures would be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So are most of the ones you're talking about single individuals or groups of two or three individuals wearing partial uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke of specific cases, and I stressed that sometimes it would be for lack of other clothing that certain parts of uniform, a military uniform, would be worn, a uniform that should one day be returned to their unit once they were invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just by looking at somebody who had a partial uniform, is there any way you could know whether or not they had been mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, nowadays you can find on our bazaars military uniforms for sale, even today. Throughout Serbia you can buy a uniform at a market and even back then there were army surplus sale points where uniforms and parts of uniforms were available to be bought, and that's how people could get hold of a uniform, not only by having a prior wartime assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Didn't you indicate, though, that you were having a problem furnishing full uniforms to the -- to the individuals that you were mobilising? Wasn't there a shortage of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. But certain types of uniform found their way to the market. They could have been bought. Among our men, some did not have uniforms. We were lacking new models of uniform. I said specifically that I took the opportunity when I failed to set up a unit made up of Albanians to distribute 400 new uniforms to other men, replacing the old uniforms that reservists wore until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure you answered my previous question, though, about whether just by looking at an individual who's wearing a partial uniform, there's no way possible, is there, you can tell whether that person has been mobilised or not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could not really tell if the man was wearing just parts of the uniform. Some men wore it for patriotic reasons, while others wore it because they had nothing else to put on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 7252 you were asked a question by Mr. Bakrac about the -- the army's ability to commandeer vehicles for use during a time of war. Was there a legal obligation to return those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Vehicles were subject to returning in the same condition in which they were received. Under regulations it was a commission that received such vehicles that again, according to regulations, the commission was supposed to return the vehicle with a full tank and with all possible damage repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, to your knowledge was that requirement complied with in Kosovo after the end of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no insight into such a large number of units, corps, or the units of the military district. Part of the vehicles were relocated outside Kosovo precisely to meet the requirements of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have a car that you drove during the conflict that was commandeered for the military use?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that car was returned to the owner who had duly issued papers certifying that his vehicle had been commandeered by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of car was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a BMW, the owner was Cerim, I can't remember the last name, from Kosovska Kamenica, and he had all the regular papers certifying that the vehicle had been commandeered and later returned after the war was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Today Mr. Bakrac was asking you some questions and one of them that he asked you about related to an event in Istok where there had been an allegation that some sort of detention facility had been set up for Albanian civilians. You indicated that an investigation was done that showed that did not exist. And in your statement at paragraph 35 you make reference to this being documented in a publication called the application of rules of the international law on armed conflicts in connection with the Yugoslav army and Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is an exhibit, Your Honours, in e-court, Exhibit P1011.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one I thing I wanted to ask you in connection with that, because you were a part of the investigating commission; correct, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the course of the investigation you learned there had been a group of Albanians, Kosovar Albanian civilians, who had left Istok and gone in the direction of Djakovica. On the way they had been intercepted by a group of what they called special forces, Serbs in uniforms wearing hats who took their vehicles and their money and jewellery and told them to go back and they had returned to Istok. Did that commission do any investigation to try and identify who those special forces were who had robbed those civilians on their way to and from Istok?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no further information as to the outcome of that report and the measures taken, if any. I believe the commission did its work very properly and submitted a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What investigation did the commission do about -- about that report of being robbed by the special forces?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We interviewed all the relevant people in Istok and concluded that there are no facts supporting the allegation that there had been a camp. Albanian civilians commended members of the army, or rather, the detachment. They praised them, and they told us that the people who had robbed them were not wearing either the uniform that I was wearing or the uniform worn by the police member of that commission. After a couple of days, the report was drafted and the chairman of the commission, Colonel Djakovic, forwarded that report and I don't know what became of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac then asked you about certain orders that you had issued. One of your orders related to governing the "life and work of the units." What authorisation did you have as head of the military district to issue orders to military territorial detachments once they had been resubordinated to the VJ or to the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even issue orders to them at the time when they were resubordinated; at least not as to how they would be used. I did inspect higher-ranking detachments to see what the situation was, just to show that I care and to see if they needed any assistance or if the unit they were resubordinated to needed any assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: However, isn't it a fact that once they were resubordinated to the Pristina Corps, the VJ had authority over them on all matters related to that new status?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. They precisely executed the orders of the commanders to whom they were subordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look briefly at 5D35.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In today's transcript at page 9, line 12, Mr. Bakrac was showing you a number of exhibits. There was one here. He was moving very quickly and I was having a hard time following, but in paragraph 2 there's a provision -- yes. Colonel, can you see paragraph 2, and it's the -- under number 2 it's actually the third paragraph. In English it's translated as: "Prevent any form of misconduct towards civilians, e.g., banning their return to populated places, especially by individuals, squad commanders, platoon commanders, et cetera." Prior to the issuance of this order, had you received reports or had any information that that kind of thing was happened; that is, that squad commanders or platoon commanders were engaging in misconduct toward civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders would be issued either on the basis of reports received from the superior command or on the basis of our own information, and that is how orders would be issued to subordinated units. They were usually spurred by reports that such things had happened somewhere. Sometimes an order would be issued as a lesson practically saying that something like that should never happen again; sometimes it would be in the form of an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 11, line 9, you told us that the military district had its own military court with a judge and prosecutor. How many cases approximately, if you know, did that military district military court investigate?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were 34 cases and some happened -- or, rather, we received some reports after the end of air-strikes, after we withdrew from the territory of Kosovo. So that figure of 34 cases stands. Maybe there were a couple of more cases. Some were turned over to the Pristina Corps, but I'm not really very familiar with this matter. Because this court was disbanded once the units were demobilised and pulled out when the Pristina Corps pulled out of Kosovo. And the cases were transferred to the court in Nis and the 3rd Army, and we had proper documentation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In a related question to that, is my understanding correct that once a military person is demobilised, if they have a case pending in military court that case gets transferred to the civilian court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think the military court follows up. I'm not quite certain about this. It could have been transferred to a military court or maybe a civilian court in the relevant region. I'm not really familiar with that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us that the Pristina Corps also had its own military court with the prosecutor and judge. Once the military territorial detachment was resubordinated to the Pristina Corps, isn't it a fact that they were responsible for discipline of those individuals in the event that they were found to be suspected of any criminal activity, and it would have been the Pristina military court that would have been investigated and prosecuted those cases?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that by doing so we would have deprived the military court belonging to that military district of its functions because it continued to work, although it was -- the military district was subordinated to the Pristina Corps. And I know that there was a good cooperation between the two courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you're not sure how that works, are you? Whether such a person would be subject to the military court of the military district or of the Pristina Corps, once they had been resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hardly give you a precise answer. I think that reservists from the military district were tried before the court of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. We'll take that up later with other witnesses. You were shown a series of documents, 5D39, 5D41, 5D42, which I believe were all regular combat reports. Do you recall those?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And those were done on a daily basis, once a day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you do that then or was that done for your signature once a day, every day, from the beginning of the conflict on the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practice and by the rules, it's the operations officer who was supposed to do that by collecting reports from the duty officer who has all the incoming information. He aggregates the information, writes a report, and submits it to me, my deputy, or whoever happens to be in charge at the command, and that persons signs it. That's how it goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's done daily?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's standard practice and our obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic then questioned you, and on page 23, line 24 of today's transcript you mentioned that the maximum strength in the entire establishment of your military district was over 12.000 men. Is that 12.000 men at any one time, any one day, or do you mean over the entire course of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is that the number varied. We had the establishment and units were supposed to be brought up to establishment. However, we had casualties, losses, and people leaving, men who were demobbed, and personnel who was relieved to serve in other duties that we referred to previously in normal life. And in view of all that, the number varied, both on the level of the military sector and the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would 12.000 then be the highest it every was on a particular day during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout that period -- well, at a certain point I remember that the figure was 12.700.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You -- at page 25, line 1, and following you were asked some questions about the military territorial detachments. Of the 24, how many of those were resubordinated to the Pristina Corps of the VJ between 24 March and 20 June 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost all of them -- well, by way of an order, military sectors were resubordinated together with all of their military detachments. At a certain point, the anti-aircraft artillery battalion was also resubordinated to the 37th Brigade, and I commanded them. And then the reconnaissance detachment was resubordinated as well to the same 37th Brigade. As I said, almost all of them. But my communications company and the staff units were never resubordinated, and this includes the military police company as well and the engineers company being a non-combat unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to look at 5D36 and page 2 of the English I think page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, while we're waiting for that to come up, when these military territorial detachments were resubordinated to the army, at that time did they receive any insignia to wear on their uniforms, or did they continue to have no insignia?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know of army members wearing any special insignia on their uniform, and the same goes for members of detachments. They had no particular insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did they have a standard VJ patch on their uniform, or was it just simply a green uniform with no patches or badges of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any patches or anything that may have been applied on their uniforms, apart from the military police. They had their own badge and various markings, including the patch they wore on the left upper arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what about on their berets? Did they have any kind of insignia, badge, or emblem?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had an insignia of the VJ on their berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In this document on the screen in front of you now under paragraph 2, item number J -- I'm just looking for your help with an abbreviation. Under J, it says: "For looking after persons displaced by activities of STG." Can you tell me what that abbreviation is, what it refers to? Are you finding that paragraph? It's under the name of Tomislav Lanicevic is underlined in that paragraph. That one, yes. Do you see where the little magnifying glass was? We'll try and enlarge that for you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Siptar terrorist groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, finally Mr. Visnjic asked you a few questions at the end, and he showed you an exhibit; I think he said it was Exhibit 3D432. It was a 29 April 1999 order that you issued about a ban on paramilitaries. Why was this order issued on this date, the 29th of April, 1999? Had you received information prior to that, that there were paramilitaries operating in your area of responsibility, that is, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally during all of my inspections I never came cross any paramilitary unit. This order was based on a previous order of the 3rd Army command, and it was forwarded down to the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your order directs the subordinate military sectors to report any such information. Did you receive any reports back in connection with this order?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have, because I was duty-bound to report up based on this order. Therefore, based on my inspection and the reports of the units, I had no knowledge of any paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give that evidence. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the next witness is K84. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I understand we have to adjust for his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll need a break for that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- but before we have the break -- Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you want, you may finish and I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you want you can finish before me, because I have something in relation of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We received supplemental information sheet from the OTP and we found it unacceptable. For example, I can give you an example. This supplemental sheet changes his statement in a way that's -- that it's not acceptable. It's not correction; it's changing. For example in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 83, it's completely different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Lukic. Why are you interrupting, Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm interrupting, Your Honour, because this witness is subject to protective measures. I anticipate when he starts reading out aspects of what his previous statements were going to be, it will tend to identify this witness. So I would ask if we're going to have this discussion we would have it in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't realise this was your witness and not Mr. -- Mr. Lukic, is that a risk that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- will arise?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. If you have in front of you this supplemental sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't have the supplemental sheet, so I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then, if we need closed session, maybe we can deal with this after the break when we are in the closed session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we won't be in closed session until it's necessary. But what I'm being told is that the Prosecution are alert to what you're about to raise and they're fearful that that might in some way undermine the protective measures. So we will, to ensure that that does not happen, go into private session for the purpose of this discussion.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are if in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While the court was in private session, a decision was made to hear the evidence of the witness K86 in closed session. In relation to the last witness, Mr. Pesic, the Prosecution made clear in re-examination that paragraph 35 of his statement refers to a document which is Exhibit 1011. It's not clear from what happened there, Mr. Hannis, the extent to which you consider that that ought to be an exhibit in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it's necessary to be an exhibit in the case. I don't think it's necessary at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a long and complicated document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. And this incident that this witness talks about is only one small portion of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's exhibited purely for the purpose of making sense of the question which you asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. We will adjourn now and resume at ten past 6.00, and we will be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of November, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
